title.rendered: Pray As You Go | A Companion to Teach Me How to Pray

excerpt.rendered: Nehemiah fired off a lightning-quick prayer in the gap between the king’s question and his answer. The anchor and the current. Pray without ceasing. A companion to Teach Me How to Pray.

content.rendered:
Nehemiah was standing in the throne room of King Artaxerxes, the most powerful man on earth, with the king asking him a question that could cost him his life. In the gap between the king’s question and his own answer, Nehemiah did something that defined the whole of New Testament prayer. He fired off a lightning-quick prayer to the God of heaven. Nobody around him knew. The whole prayer took less than a second. And heaven heard it.

The Gospel For Today | Saturday, October 17, 2026 | A Companion to Teach Me How to Pray

Today’s Scripture

“Pray without ceasing.”
1 Thessalonians 5:17 (NKJV)

Today’s Message

Over the past fourteen days of the Teach Me How to Pray series we studied the dedicated prayer times of Jesus. Rising before daylight. The solitary place. The hours alone with the Father. We studied the authority He walked in because of those early-morning appointments, and we were called into the same rhythm. That teaching stands. But if we stop there, we will leave Gospelbuzz readers with half a theology of prayer. Because Paul tells the Thessalonian church, in a sentence that leaves no room for scheduling, “Pray without ceasing.” Not pray at six in the morning and tick the box. Not pray on Sunday and move on. Pray without ceasing. Prayer is not merely a scheduled appointment with the Father. It is a continuous conversation that runs through the whole of the believer’s day.

Think of it as the anchor and the current. The anchor is the dedicated prayer time Jesus modelled in Mark 1:35. The quiet enclosure. The solitary place. The deliberate, structured appointment with the Father where the believer receives direction, receives strength, and settles the day’s agenda. The current is Paul’s “pray without ceasing”, the constant, moment-by-moment conversation that flows through every room the believer walks into. Both are prayer. Both are real. Both are heard. And the believer who develops both begins to live the way the Bible actually describes. Nehemiah is the perfect picture. He had a months-long season of structured fasting and prayer in Nehemiah 1. Then when the critical moment came in Nehemiah 2:4-5, standing before the king, he fired off an in-the-moment prayer in the silent gap of a conversation. Both were heard. Both were answered. The anchor and the current worked together.

This is the concept of Pray As You Go. Prayer can happen anywhere, at any time, in any posture. In the quiet moments between meetings. While driving the kids to school. In the kitchen while cooking. In the middle of a difficult conversation, muttered under the breath. In the queue at the supermarket. On the walk from the car to the office. In the pause before answering a hard email. On a flight at 35,000 feet. These short, continuous prayers, some whispered, some silent, some spoken aloud, keep the believer in constant communion with the Father all day long. The Passion Translation of 1 Thessalonians 5:17 renders it with a vividness that captures the heart: “Make your life a prayer” (1 Thessalonians 5:17 TPT). The Amplified Bible Classic Edition adds: “Be unceasing in prayer [praying perseveringly]” (1 Thessalonians 5:17 AMPC). Make your life a prayer. Prayer stops being an item on the to-do list and becomes the atmosphere the believer breathes.

The Many Shapes of Prayer

Jesus Himself prayed in many shapes. He prayed early (Mark 1:35). He prayed all night (Luke 6:12). He prayed with thanksgiving before meals (Matthew 14:19). He prayed before raising the dead (John 11:41-42). He prayed in agony in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). He prayed on the cross (Luke 23:34, 46). The prayer life of Jesus was not one shape. It was many. And the New Testament teaches the believer that there are many kinds of prayer, each with its own purpose.

Supplication. Asking the Father for specific needs (Philippians 4:6). This is the most familiar form for most believers, bringing requests to the Father.

Intercession. Praying on behalf of others. The whole of John 17 is intercession, as Jesus prayed for His disciples and for every believer who would come after. The believer, as part of the royal priesthood, is called to intercede for family, church, city, and nation.

Thanksgiving. Gratitude for what has already been given (Philippians 4:6, 1 Thessalonians 5:18). The believer who prays with thanksgiving is already receiving by faith what has been promised.

Praise and Worship. Adoration of who God is in Himself, apart from what He gives. The Psalms are full of this. Jesus modelled it in Matthew 11:25.

Agreement. Two or more praying together. Jesus promised in Matthew 18:19 that whatever two agree on the earth concerning anything they ask, it will be done for them by the Father in heaven.

Spiritual Warfare. Enforcing Kingdom authority against the enemy. Speaking to mountains (Mark 11:23). Resisting the devil so he flees (James 4:7). Standing against principalities and powers (Ephesians 6:12).

Declaration, or Declarative Prayer. This is the prayer where the believer takes what God has said and speaks it over things, situations, people, and circumstances. The pattern comes directly from Ezekiel 37, where the Lord commanded the prophet to prophesy to the valley of dry bones based on what God had already said about them. The bones came together, the sinews and flesh came upon them, and the breath of God entered them, because the prophet spoke what God had spoken. The believer takes a word God has already declared in Scripture, acknowledges it as true, personalises it as their own, and then proclaims it over their life. For example, Jesus said in John 14:20, “At that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you in Me, and I in you.” A declarative prayer takes that word and proclaims it: “I declare and acknowledge that I am in Christ and Christ is in me, and we are in the Father. Therefore, my location and abode is in Christ, in God. Nothing can hurt or harm me.” Jesus modelled this pattern throughout His earthly ministry, speaking to the mountain, the storm, the fig tree, the leper, Lazarus, each declaration grounded in the Father’s revealed will. The whole of the coming How to Declare as Jesus Did series on Gospelbuzz will unpack this prayer form in depth.

Prayer in the Spirit, Prayer in Tongues. A Spirit-enabled prayer language given to the believer when the Holy Spirit is received. Jude 20 says, “But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit.” 1 Corinthians 14:14-15 says, “For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays… I will pray with the spirit, and I will also pray with the understanding.” Romans 8:26 describes the Spirit interceding through the believer “with groanings which cannot be uttered.” Prayer in tongues bypasses the limits of the natural understanding and allows the believer to pray according to the Father’s perfect will even when the believer does not know what to pray.

Fasting and Prayer. Prayer joined to a deliberate denying of the body. Jesus taught it as a given in Matthew 6:16-18, saying “when you fast” rather than “if you fast.” The early church practised it (Acts 13:2-3) and the Lord spoke to them in it.

Contemplative, Listening Prayer. Stillness before the Lord. “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). Elijah heard the still, small voice only after the wind, the earthquake, and the fire had passed (1 Kings 19:11-13). Sometimes the deepest praying is the quietest.

None of these cancel the others. They work together. For Gospelbuzz readers today, wherever you are reading this from, in Lagos or London or Manila or Nairobi or Sao Paulo, the Christian life is meant to be bathed in prayer of many shapes, flowing continuously through every hour of every day. Anchor your day in the solitary place. Then let the current of Pray As You Go run through everything else. That is the full picture Jesus and the New Testament are showing us.

Prayer (Anchor and Current)

The Anchor. Father, I thank You that You have called me into both a dedicated appointment and a continuous conversation. In this quiet place today, I give You my first attention. Speak. Direct. Fill. I receive from You before I give to anyone else.

The Current. And through the rest of this day, Father, I ask You to make my life a prayer. In the car. In the queue. Between the meetings. At the kitchen sink. In the walk from one room to the next. Let my spirit remain in constant conversation with Your Spirit, so that I never leave Your presence, even for a moment.

Many Shapes. Teach me to use every shape of prayer You have given: supplication, intercession, thanksgiving, praise, agreement, warfare, declaration, prayer in the Spirit, fasting, and listening. Make me fluent in all of them, so that whatever the moment calls for, I know how to pray.

In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Declaration

My life is a prayer. I anchor my day in the solitary place and I live the rest of my day in constant conversation with the Father. Every room I walk into, I walk into praying. Every moment is an opportunity to lift my spirit to Him. I pray without ceasing.
